title: Inside Stephen Miller’s aggressive first week as Trump’s chief of staff
content: Stephen Miller spent his first week as President Donald Trump’s chief of staff sending a clear message across the West Wing: He’s no Susie Wiles. The new top aide has sought to quickly consolidate control within the White House and distance himself from his ousted predecessor, signaling plans to overhaul key procedures and personnel as the administration girds for a final two years of political warfare. Miller’s aggressive early moves, including issuing a pair of memos purporting to empower Cabinet secretaries and restrict lobbyists’ influence, surprised many White House officials and allies who interpreted them as direct shots at Wiles — and a response to criticism in the MAGA base over how she directed the first two years of Trump’s presidency, leading up to November’s disastrous midterm losses. “Stephen’s in the driver’s seat now,” said one Trump ally. “It’s going to be very, very different — extremely different.” Since taking over as chief of staff on Monday, Miller has announced changes to the administration’s communications strategy, which is aimed at giving Cabinet leaders more autonomy to shape and deliver their own messaging. He’s instituted a ban on White House meetings with lobbyists without prior approval. And he’s streamlined some staffing structures in the West Wing that will effectively route greater decision making authority directly through him, while relying on a tight circle of allies — notably including his wife Katie, who people familiar with the matter said had played a central role in pressing Trump allies to support Miller’s candidacy for the chief of staff job ahead of Wiles’ ouster. A White House official said Katie Miller has zero involvement in White House decision making. The changes represent the first steps in a broader effort by Miller to effectively accelerate Trump’s MAGA agenda over the final stage of his presidency. Some people familiar with his early moves described the 41-year-old loyalist as attempting to set the parameters for what Trump wants to get done — and then pushing officials across the administration to fulfill those goals as rapidly as possible. It’s a familiar strategy for Miller, who has spent the last two years taking that exact approach to accelerate a controversial immigration crackdown. “He understands how government works and what the powers and levers of government are,” one Trump adviser said of Miller, “and he knows what the president is trying to accomplish.” While the new tack has won praise among some in the administration who had chafed over Wiles’ efforts to tightly control the administration’s messaging and policy priorities, some Miller skeptics worry it could end up turning an already freewheeling White House even more chaotic. His decision to revoke a Wiles policy that every appearance and announcement across the administration first get approval from the West Wing has been particularly polarizing. One administration official called the prior rule “suffocating,” but another person close to the White House worried about the practical effects of a White House — particularly one led by an always-opinionated Trump — with less oversight. Under the new approach, Cabinet secretaries will have more direct access to Miller and Trump — a change meant to allow the president to communicate more freely with his top officials. Yet that could also herald a return to the unruly, knives-out atmosphere of his first term, when Trump’s Cabinet members routinely undermined and fought with one another in an effort win his favor. In a statement, White House spokesman Taylor Rogers praised Miller as “a loyal aide to President Trump for more than a decade” who “is trusted by the President’s entire Cabinet.” “In his role as Chief of Staff, he will continue working to implement President Trump’s populist agenda on behalf of the nation’s working people,” Rogers added. Still, despite Miller’s commitment for a renewed effort to crack down on unauthorized media disclosures, large swaths of the administration spent the last week consumed by infighting and leaks over the fallout from revelations that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a women suspected of having links to Chinese intelligence. “This is a Trump-centric White House. The system was designed to enable a top-down White House centric operation, where the agencies move on the president’s America First policy,” that source said of Wiles’ communications’ system, which aimed to head off major disagreements and keep all of Trump’s aides aligned. “So are we not a White House-centric administration now?” US Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has been among those particularly invigorated by the changeover, people who have spoken to him said. He believes that Miller will supercharge his “Make America Healthy Again” agenda after months of White House stalling on a series of key policies, according to those people. While Kennedy has been publicly complimentary of Wiles’ tenure, the decision to sideline those priorities frustrated those around him, prompted his top adviser to quit and spurred backlash among some of the MAHA movement’s most vocal supporters. But others across the Trump administration have been unnerved by the lengths at which Miller has gone to publicly change Wiles’ policies. The moves sowed immediate concerns over what the new regime would look like and who would remain a part of it, with one official describing staffers as walking on eggshells, unsure if their jobs were safe. Miller has not yet held an all-staff meeting since taking over on Monday, primarily because he’s not yet finished making all of his planned changes to White House personnel, a White House official said. Miller’s second memo, meanwhile, appeared to be an even more direct effort to separate himself from Wiles’ tenure. The missive barred staffers from meeting with lobbyists on White House grounds without permission — a rule likely to have little impact on lobbyists’ ability to reach Trump staffers, but that nevertheless one that served as an implicit rebuke of Wiles and her team. A former lobbyist, Wiles and some of her closest allies have faced harsh criticism from the MAGA right over allegations that they granted outsized influence to lobbying firms and wealthy donors who gave money to Republicans ahead of the midterms. The White House has frequently denied that outside interests had any power to shape policy decisions. But since his promotion, Miller’s allies have stressed his own personal skepticism of lobbyists, contending that he’s long been unmoved by any arguments that don’t directly advance the Trump agenda that he’s long played a central role in developing. “Stephen is a guy who isn’t moved by connections; he’s a guy who’s moved by policy arguments,” said Hunter Morgen, a lobbyist at Ballard Partners who worked with Miller during the first Trump administration. “He can be moved on issues, but you need to have the tightest, strongest argument and also be willing to concede points.” To that end, the White House under Miller is expected to double down on Trump’s efforts to expand his executive authority, rebuild his populist coalition, and cement his legacy, despite voters’ widespread rejection of his and his party’s governing choices less than two weeks ago. Miller and other Trump officials have sought to prepare a range of executive actions ahead of next year that the administration can take to unilaterally advance its agenda and try to re-energize the MAGA base. In the meantime, the White House sent a pair of clear signals in recent days that it plans to fight any efforts by the incoming Democratic majorities in the House and Senate to bog it down with investigations. In the hours after Miller’s ascension to chief of staff, White House officials worked to shield Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth from impeachment, ultimately rallying enough Republican support to defeat the measure. The White House then separately issued an extraordinary letter threatening congressional Democrats who planned to investigate the administration that they could soon face criminal probes of their own. In the days since Republicans’ midterm drubbing, some Trump allies and advisers have counseled the president and Miller to leave the door open to working with Democrats, arguing that they may be able to find ways to advance parts of the administration’s agenda. But while Trump has continued to publicly suggest he could strike deals with Democrats, there is far less private belief that the effort will amount to anything, said the people familiar with the matter. They cast doubt on the idea Democratic lawmakers could ever make the kinds of concessions necessary to win over the president and Miller. Instead, Trump is more likely to wage a lengthy, contentious battle over the next two years to cement his legacy — and bet that Miller can manage the sprawling administration well enough to rack up a few victories. “If you have (Democrats), in essence, saying they’re going to war with you, then you want a wartime consigliere,” said Newt Gingrich, a close Trump ally and former GOP House speaker. “And Steve Miller is a great wartime consigliere.”

title: Judge halts Trump plan to redevelop Washington, DC, golf course
content: A federal judge halted President Donald Trump’s plan to renovate a municipal golf court in Washington, DC , on Saturday night, issuing a temporary order that requires the administration keep the course open after Trump said it would be closed on Sunday for the overhaul. US District Judge Ana C. Reyes said the administration’s push to revamp East Potomac Golf Links into the championship course Trump desires – one of several construction projects the president has sought as part of his effort to remake Washington to his tastes and leave a legacy – likely violated environmental law and ran afoul of procedural guardrails for executive branch actions. She said the Justice Department’s arguments in the litigation, where it claimed that the November 15 closure was happening for safety reasons, were “pretextual.” “The Government proposes to close a historic park, daily enjoyed by Washingtonians of all stripes, indefinitely,” Reyes wrote, finding that the closure would “irreparably harm” the plaintiffs in the case, individual golfers and preservationists. In a statement following the ruling, the DOJ said it will “always vociferously defend the Trump Administration’s agenda in court.” “The Court has acknowledged that the National Park Service can limit access to its facilities where the public is at risk of harm,” a DOJ spokesperson told CNN. “Nothing in the Court’s order precludes planning for the development of a world class golf course to continue.” It’s the latest development in a monthslong battle between Reyes and the Trump administration – one that has prompted Trump smearing the judge on social media and suggestions from Reyes that government attorneys may have misled her. The Justice Department has unsuccessfully tried to remove her from the case, brought by preservationists and golfers seeking to stop the redevelopment arguing that changing the course would run afoul of federal environmental regulations and diminish public access. Trump, an avid golfer, first publicly proposed the idea of taking over and expanding the municipal golf course in May and was soon thereafter seen touring the grounds with Interior Secretary Doug Burgum and Tom Fazio, a well known golf designer who worked on several of Trump’s private courses. The president initially said work on the East Potomac Links would begin September 1, which accelerated the legal challenge. Saturday, the president continued to promote the project and posted photos of what he has called “Trash Island.” “Unfortunately, Judge Ana Reyes doesn’t want us to quickly and inexpensively fix up the Course which is, also, very dangerous — The Fairways are far too close together,” Trump said in a social media post . “When you walk down the corridors of Trash Island, you don’t hear the sound of the running Potomac, all you hear is the sound of people screaming, ‘FORE!’” In recent months, Reyes has expressed growing frustration with the administration. In October, Reyes issued a stark order blocking tree removal and imposing new notice requirements after over 400 trees were removed from the course with minimal notice. “More than just being upset and furious right now, I am just beyond disappointed with the government,” Reyes said during that hearing. The administration claimed the removals were necessary and not tied to Trump’s desired renovation, a claim Reyes said she was “skeptical” of in last month’s hearing. “The question goes to whether or not I have been lied to, whether I have been lied to in declarations about the plans, whether I have been lied to about the timing of things,” Reyes told Justice Department lawyers at the time. The legal rationale of her ruling Saturday night turned on the National Park Service’s failures to take certain steps before overhaul that she found to be required by law – such has providing notice to the public of the plan and soliciting their comment on it. “Notice-and-comment rulemaking is not impracticable merely because NPS wishes to accommodate President Trump and close the Park by November 15,” she wrote. While the stakes surrounding the course have been comparatively low when put up against other legal battles roiling the Trump administration, the case has been one of several in which the administration has bristled at complying with court orders. Other projects, such as the president’s efforts to rename the Kennedy Center, build a triumphal arch on the banks of the Potomac and construct a ballroom, are also all facing legal challenges. This story was updated with additional information. CNN’s Aleena Fayaz contributed to this report.

title: US has floated Ukraine ceding Donbas for Nato membership, Zelensky says
content:
US negotiators have touted the idea of Ukraine withdrawing its remaining forces from the eastern Donbas region in exchange for Nato membership, President Volodymyr Zelensky has said.
The US has not confirmed Zelensky's comments, and a US official told the BBC "many ideas continue to be discussed but any final deal will have to be agreed to by both parties".
The Ukrainian leader's comments came after US envoys met Russian President Vladimir Putin and Zelensky as part of US efforts to end the war between Russia and Ukraine.
Kyiv has long sought membership of the military alliance, but this has previously been opposed by the US and others while Russia has said another Nato member on its border is unacceptable.
Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. It controls most of the industrial region of Donbas and Zelensky has consistently said Ukraine is unwilling to give up sovereign territory.
"The Americans raised a question: 'What if Ukraine joins Nato? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?' This was the first time this had been raised," Zelensky said in remarks released by his office on Saturday.
He went on to say that if he received a specific proposal that contained security guarantees, no constraints on Ukraine's military and funds to rebuild the country, he would put it to a referendum.
US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff travelled to the Irish capital, Dublin, on Thursday to meet Zelensky, after a round of talks with Putin in Moscow.
Comments by both Putin and Kremlin officials suggest that Russia's position on the war has not shifted. It has previously proposed limits on the size of Ukraine's military, territorial concessions and Kyiv's guaranteed neutrality as conditions of a peace deal.
Ukraine has rejected these, arguing that such constraints would hamper its ability to stave off any future invasion.
Other Nato members apart from the US are wary of membership for Ukraine - and it is understood that Ukraine itself sees that as unrealistic.
The Kremlin has always been fiercely opposed, too. It is one reason why Russia started this war in the first place.
It is possible the American envoys were exploring Ukraine's "red lines" when it comes to occupied land in the Donbas. Zelensky said recently that the US mediators believed Kyiv only had to cede territory to achieve peace and were applying pressure, keen to do a deal as soon as possible.
Ukraine is sure that Russia's ambitions are far greater and has long seen Nato as its only sure protection.
So it is also possible that Zelensky made this suggestion public in order to re-open a discussion that had been considered all but closed.
He maintains that the idea is now "back on the agenda" as part of an "extremely difficult conversation" on European security.
It also looks like Ukrainian push-back against Russia's renewed hardline stance. Moscow now talks about a "new European security architecture", which is long-standing Russian code for a weaker Nato.
The issue appears to have been the main focus at the latest round of talks between Ukraine, Russia and the US in Abu Dhabi this week.
Hours after Zelensky's remarks, Jared Kushner appeared keen to dampen down any US offer of Nato membership for Ukraine, urging "confidentiality" in a sensitive process.
He said that "maximalist" proposals had been reported from the negotiations, along with "strong political rhetoric".

final_quality.reason: This article reports a significant development in the Ukraine-Russia conflict, shedding light on US-NATO-Ukraine negotiations and potential territorial concessions. The article provides specific quotes from Zelensky and context on the previous negotiations, making it a substantive and important contribution to the category.
